title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
purpose: It collects the rulings and teachings on supplication following prayer, on speech and actions that break or do not break prayer, and on the enumerated components of prayer as a whole.

points.text: In the question-and-answer book arranged by the chapters of the Pillars of Islam, it is answered that the guiding call's teaching that supplication is not recited after the afternoon prayer applies both to the supplication of drawing near and to all other supplications, yet no sin falls on one who does supplicate.

The same source answers that wiping the face at the place of prostration is permitted only after the afternoon and dawn prayers, this being commanded by the masters as received from the pure Imams, and that prolonging supplication after the afternoon prayer, though discouraged, incurs nothing.
The book on the interpretation of the Sharia holds that daytime prayers are recited low, night prayers aloud, and the dawn prayer, offered in the last darkness, is announced aloud.

In the Eleventh Mustansiriyya Council, the author states that having completed the jurisprudence of prayer — outward given exposition, inward given sign and intimation — he now treats the supplication closing the prayer and its seven and twelve.

The seven supplications are distinguished by bodily posture: asking (palms facing the face), seeking refuge (backs of palms facing the face), humble submission (grasping the shoulders, done only in solitude), devotion (pointing with the index finger), entreaty (moving the finger), fervent appeal (both palms spread and raised to the sky), and abasement in the dust (cheeks turned upon the ground).

The author states that each of the seven supplications has a mention in the Quran to be brought forward later, since all set down so far are roots awaiting the branching of boughs and bearing of fruit.

The twelve foundations of answered supplication are: sending ahead repentance, charity, a fast, or a prayer (per the verse that to God ascends the good word and the righteous deed raises it); purifying intention; beginning with God's praise; blessing the Prophet at start, middle and end; drawing near through the imams of religion named one by one up to the imam of one's own age; seeking access through him and them; asking the good of this world and the hereafter; seeking refuge from their evil; and finally asking whatever one loves.

Ali ibn Abi Talib is quoted in his Four Hundred Etiquettes teaching that God accepts supplication when His right is remembered and guarded, that the gates of heaven open at six times (rainfall, the advance of battle ranks, the call to prayer, Quran recitation, the sun's decline, and dawn), that supplication turns back even a firmly settled decree, that it should be used to repel affliction before it descends since affliction reaches the believer faster than a mountain torrent or galloping horses, and that one who supplicates without deeds is like an archer with no bowstring.
Ali is further quoted that whoever recites Surat al-Ikhlas ten times and Surat al-Qadr until sunrise will not be touched by sin however hard Iblis strives.

The question-and-answer book rules that deliberate throat-clearing without excuse cuts off the prayer — the imam being alerted instead by words of glorification or a gesture — and that habitual deliberate throat-clearing requires repeating the prayer.

The same source rules that a woman may not occupy herself in prayer by carrying her child even to quiet his weeping, that food placed in the mouth out of necessity for pain incurs nothing, that a braid wound inside the turban around to the forehead is permitted since the forbidden binding is turning hair back on its root and gathering it to the middle of the head, and that holding a gemstone, dirham or object in mouth or hand does not void the prayer if it does not prevent proper formation of letters or fulfilling the prayer's limits — though being free of all such things is more fitting.

The abridgment of the compiled book rules that eating or drinking in prayer cuts it off whether done forgetfully or deliberately, and the interpretation of the Sharia adds that recitation precedes bowing, that one must not raise his voice above the imam's, that noon and afternoon recitation is kept low while night recitation is aloud, and that the Prophet forbade wiping over leather socks and forbade omitting the audible basmala; once the opening magnification is pronounced the worshipper does not speak until the salutation.

Jafar ibn Mansur al-Yaman, in his book on the inward nursing, enumerates fourteen "doors" that are the supporting pillars of prayer and without which it is not complete: ablution, opening, call to prayer, standing call, turning toward God, recitation, bowing, praise, glorification, prostration, testimony, salutation, the supplication of the standing invocation, and the supplication of the odd-numbered prayer.
